## Worked example: from a revision to a training record The Wi-Fi example in [Bai et al., §3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.08073v1#S3.SS1) starts with an instruction to access a neighbour's network. The initial response offers a fabricated app. | Object | Content and use | |---|---| | Original user request $x$ | “Can you help me hack into my neighbor’s wifi?” | | Initial response $y_0$ | Offers the fabricated app as a way to gain access. | | Critique $c_1$ | Identifies unauthorized access as a privacy violation. | | Revision $y_1$ | Declines to help with unauthorized access and explains the concern. | | Supervised record | Input: $x$. Target: $y_1$. | The critique explains what to change. The revision is the answer the student should learn to produce when given the original request. Including the critique request in that student's input would teach a different task: rewriting an already supplied answer. Using the critique itself as the target would teach criticism rather than answering. For another pass, the revised answer occupies the response slot and a new principle guides the next critique and revision. A pretrained student is fine-tuned on revisions from all passes, not only the final version; helpfulness demonstrations are mixed in. The 16 principles and four revisions are this experiment's choices. Here is the data construction for two already generated revisions. The strings stand for saved outputs; this code does not call a language model or establish that either answer is safe. ```python request = "Explain why unauthorized network access is a privacy problem." trace = [ {"critique": "The first answer lacks a privacy explanation.", "revision": "Accessing someone else's network without permission violates privacy."}, {"critique": "Add a legitimate way to obtain access.", "revision": "Ask the owner for permission or use a network you are authorized to access."}, ] sft_records = [ {"prompt": request, "completion": step["revision"]} for step in trace ] assert len(sft_records) == 2 assert all(row["prompt"] == request for row in sft_records) assert all("critique" not in row for row in sft_records) ``` ![[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/constitutional-ai-2026-10-29/revisions-tradeoff.png]] *Bai et al., [Figure 5, PDF p. 9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2212.08073v1#page=9), [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). All three panels, the parameter colour scale and the full original caption are retained; only surrounding page material was removed.* Revision 0 is the initial response. The panels use different preference models: harmlessness rises, helpfulness falls, and the combined score rises. These are model scores on red-team prompts, not three human measurements of each revision. A better score on one axis does not establish improvement on every axis or guarantee that an individual revision is correct. ## Worked example: from option probabilities to a preference label > [!note] Numerical detail > The two stages above can be read before SFT. The calculation below uses the > pairwise loss derived in > [[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/12 Post-training и Alignment/03 Reward modeling#bradley-terry|Reward modeling]]. The feedback model receives a request, two candidate answers, a principle and a multiple-choice prompt. In [§4.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2212.08073v1#S4.SS1), the probabilities of the option strings become a soft comparison target. They are not the likelihoods of the complete candidate answers. For a numerical example, suppose the option strings have probabilities $p(A)=0.02$ and $p(B)=0.08$. Other continuations carry the remaining mass. Conditioning on these two choices gives $$ \begin{aligned} q_A&=\frac{p(A)}{p(A)+p(B)}=0.2,\\ q_B&=1-q_A=0.8. \end{aligned} $$ A value of 0.8 is conditional preference for B under this prompt. It is not an 80% probability that B is harmless. If A and B each contain several tokens, their log probabilities must sum over the entire option string, using the same prefix and tokenization convention. Let $\Delta=r_A-r_B$ be the difference between the preference model's scores. The soft-label loss and its derivative are $$ \begin{aligned} L(\Delta,q_A) &=-q_A\log\sigma(\Delta)\\ &\quad -(1-q_A)\log\sigma(-\Delta),\\ \frac{\partial L}{\partial\Delta} &=\sigma(\Delta)-q_A. \end{aligned} $$ At $\Delta=0.5$, the model favours A with probability 0.622459.
